Issued at 300 AM CST Sun Nov 15 2026

An omega blocking pattern is in the process of breaking down 
early this morning as it is being undercut by a progressive 
closed low over the Texas Panhandle. A lower amplitude mid 
level shortwave is also preparing to eject off the Northern 
Rockies early this morning and will cross the region today, 
producing no precipitation and not even much in the way of 
cloud cover. An underlying surface trough will also meander 
eastward into western North Dakota this afternoon, with breezy 
southerly winds ahead of through and lighter westerly winds 
behind. Highs this afternoon should mostly be in the 50s. Upper
level ridging is forecast to resume over the Northern Plains on
Monday as a trough digs into the western CONUS. This should 
give us the warmest day of the forecast period with highs 
mostly in the mid 50s to lower 60s. The western trough 
approaches the Rockies on Tuesday, turning flow aloft over the 
Northern Plains to the southwest. It will remain dry on 
Tuesday, but increased cloud cover and surface flow becoming 
southerly to easterly are projected to cool high temperatures 
into the mid 40s to mid 50s.

There is strong ensemble consensus that the upstream trough 
will eject into the Northern Plains on Wednesday, but there is 
still considerable uncertainty on its strength and to some 
extent, the trajectory of strongest forcing. Ensemble clusters 
are heavily separated by system core. Key takeaways from 
cluster analysis are that the GEFS strongly favors a more 
potent and progressive wave through the Dakotas, while the 
ECMWF ensemble prefers a lower amplitude wave with the 
strongest forcing closer to Nebraska. All solutions want to 
bring light precipitation across the state Wednesday through 
Wednesday night, with higher chances north than south. Mean 
maximum QPF within the state is only around 0.1" for ECMWF-
heavy clusters, but closer to 0.25" in their counterparts. It 
should be noted that even though 6-hourly NBM PoPs are only 10 
to 50 percent, raw ensemble probabilities for measurable 
precipitation in a 24-hour period are closer to 50 to 90 
percent. As the wave and its attendant surface low progress 
northeastward, cooler air will be dragged into the state. Highs
on Wednesday are only forecast to reach the mid to upper 30s in
the northwest, but could still approach 50 in the southern 
James River Valley. A transition from rain to snow could begin 
as early as late Wednesday afternoon in the far west, with the 
rain/snow transition line progressing eastward through 
Wednesday night, but perhaps not as quickly as the departure of
precipitation. The progressive nature of the system should 
greatly limit accumulating snow potential. Probabilities for 
measurable snowfall with this system range from around 10 
percent from southwest to north central North Dakota to near 50
percent in the far northwest corner of the state, and the 
lowest membership cluster (less than 20 percent of the total 
membership) is far more aggressive with snow probabilities than
the other 3.

Ensembles are in agreement with a transitory ridge keeping 
Thursday dry, but it will remain cooler with highs only 
projected in the upper 30s to mid 40s. Attention then turns to 
the next western CONUS trough and its evolution Friday through 
the weekend. The GEFS is nearly unanimous that the trough will 
translate through the Northern Plains as an open, progressive 
wave Friday into Saturday. This solution (hereafter referred to
as Scenario 1) is favored by 60-65 percent of the total 
ensemble membership, as the ECMWF and Canadian ensembles are 
much more dispersive. The other, lower membership outcome 
(Scenario 2) brings a slower, deeper, and more southerly wave 
into the Northern/Central Plains late Friday through Saturday. 
But there are two distinct potential outcomes within Scenario 2:
an ECMWF-only solution that would keep the highest QPF south of
North Dakota (Scenario 2a), and a slightly lower probability
outcome mostly driven by Canadian ensemble members that would
bring much higher QPF across much of the state (Scenario 2b).
Scenario 1 would favor higher QPF in eastern North Dakota
compared to the west, but still with lower maxima than Scenario
2b. NBM-based high temperatures are still in the mid 30s to mid
40s on Friday, then lower to upper 30s on Saturday. But raw
ensemble probabilities for sub-freezing temperatures at midday
Saturday are medium to high (except for the dry Scenario 2a).
This means that precipitation from this system could fall more
as snow than rain, but it is still difficult to draw any
conclusions on potential snow amounts given the forecast time
range and uncertainty, especially with a 20 percent chance of
little to no precipitation at all (Scenario 2a). Scenario 1
